quiz_item.scenario_prompt: What is the single most critical safety rule when choosing a location to erect an outdoor amateur radio mast or wire antenna?
quiz_item.question: What is the single most critical safety rule when choosing a location to erect an outdoor amateur radio mast or wire antenna?
options: A. Mount the antenna directly onto an electric utility pole so the coax shield shares the power company ground wire.
B. String dipole wires directly underneath high-voltage overhead distribution lines to shield the receiver from lightning.
C. Erect the mast only during rainstorms so moist soil improves radio-frequency grounding.
D. Locate the antenna and mast far enough from all overhead power lines that even if the mast or wire falls in any direction, it cannot come within 10 feet of a power line.
choices: A. Mount the antenna directly onto an electric utility pole so the coax shield shares the power company ground wire.
B. String dipole wires directly underneath high-voltage overhead distribution lines to shield the receiver from lightning.
C. Erect the mast only during rainstorms so moist soil improves radio-frequency grounding.
D. Locate the antenna and mast far enough from all overhead power lines that even if the mast or wire falls in any direction, it cannot come within 10 feet of a power line.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Locate the antenna and mast far enough from all overhead power lines that even if the mast or wire falls in any direction, it cannot come within 10 feet of a power line.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Contact between an antenna or mast and overhead electrical power lines is a leading cause of fatal electrocution in radio operations; antennas must never be placed where they could fall onto or near power lines.

requirements.req_text: Amateur and Professional Radio. Do ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Amateur Radio. Do ALL of the following: (1) Tell why the FCC has an amateur radio service. Describe activities that amateur radio operators can do on the air, once they have earned an amateur radio license. (2) Explain differences between the Technician, General, and Extra Class license requirements and privileges. Explain who administers amateur radio exams. (3) Explain at least five Q signals or amateur radio terms. (4) Explain how you would make an emergency call on voice or Morse code. Resources: How To Use Your VHF Marine Radio To Call for Help in a Boat Emergency (video) Ham Radio Disaster Messaging Demo (video) Using Ham Radio To Call for Help in an Emergency, What You Should Do! (video) (5) Explain the differences between handheld, mobile, and base station transceivers and their uses. Explain the use of amateur radio repeaters. (6) Using proper call signs, Q signals, and abbreviations, carry on a 10-minute real or simulated amateur radio contact using voice, Morse code, or digital mode. Properly log the real or simulated amateur radio contact, and record the signal report. Note: Licensed amateur radio operators may substitute five QSL cards as evidence of contacts with five amateur radio operators. (b) Option B, Radio Broadcasting. Do ALL of the following: (1) Discuss with your counselor FCC broadcast regulations. Include power levels, frequencies, and the regulations for low-power stations. (2) Prepare a program schedule for radio station "KBSA" of exactly one-half hour, including music, news, commercials, and proper station identification. Record your program on audiotape or in a digital audio format, using proper techniques. (3) Listen to and properly log 15 broadcast stations. Determine the program format and target audience for five of these stations. (4) Explain to your counselor at least eight terms used in commercial broadcasting, such as segue, cut, fade, continuity, remote, Emergency Alert System, network, cue, dead air, PSA, and playlist. (5) Discuss with your counselor alternative radio platforms such as internet streaming, satellite radio, and podcasts. (c) Option C, Shortwave and Medium-Wave Listening. Do ALL of the following: (1) Listen across several shortwave bands for four one-hour periods-at least one period during daylight hours and at least one period at night. Log the stations properly and locate them geographically on a map, globe, or web-based mapping service. (2) Listen to several medium-wave stations for two one-hour periods, one period during daylight hours and one period at night. Log the stations properly and locate them on a map, globe, or web-based mapping service. (3) Compare your daytime and nighttime logs; note the frequencies on which your selected stations were loudest during each session. Explain differences in the signal strength from one period to the next. (4) Compare your medium-wave broadcast station logs and explain why some distant stations are heard at your location only during the night. (5) Demonstrate listening to a radio broadcast using a smartphone/cell phone. Include international broadcasts in your demonstration. (d) Option D, Amateur Radio Direction Finding. Do ALL of the following: (1) Describe amateur radio direction finding and explain why direction finding is important as both an activity and in competition. (2) Describe what frequencies and equipment are used for ARDF or fox hunting. (3) Build a simple directional antenna for either of the two frequencies used in ARDF. (4) Participate in a simple fox hunt using your antenna along with a provided receiver. (5) Show, on a map, how you located the "fox" using your receiver. (e) Option E, Family Radio Service (FRS) and General Mobile Radio Service (GMRS) Walkie Talkies. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain what the Family Radio Service (FRS) and General Mobile Radio Service (GMRS) are and how they are different from each other, from other commercial two-way radios, and from Citizens Band (CB) and amateur radio (ham). (2) Explain each of the following for using a FRS radio or GMRS walkie talkie: (a) Is any type of license needed to use these radios? If so: what kind? (b) What radio frequencies are used and how is information encoded? (c) How much power can be used when transmitting? (d) What type of antenna can be used? (e) What is the effective range and what limits it? (f) What are common everyday uses for these radios? (g) How can these radios be useful in an emergency? (3) Use the FRS radios or GMRS walkie talkies with family, friends, or Scouts on a hike, at an event, or in a team game. Discuss what you learned with your counselor.

requirements.description: Amateur and Professional Radio. Do ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Amateur Radio. Do ALL of the following: (1) Tell why the FCC has an amateur radio service. Describe activities that amateur radio operators can do on the air, once they have earned an amateur radio license. (2) Explain differences between the Technician, General, and Extra Class license requirements and privileges. Explain who administers amateur radio exams. (3) Explain at least five Q signals or amateur radio terms. (4) Explain how you would make an emergency call on voice or Morse code. Resources: How To Use Your VHF Marine Radio To Call for Help in a Boat Emergency (video) Ham Radio Disaster Messaging Demo (video) Using Ham Radio To Call for Help in an Emergency, What You Should Do! (video) (5) Explain the differences between handheld, mobile, and base station transceivers and their uses. Explain the use of amateur radio repeaters. (6) Using proper call signs, Q signals, and abbreviations, carry on a 10-minute real or simulated amateur radio contact using voice, Morse code, or digital mode. Properly log the real or simulated amateur radio contact, and record the signal report. Note: Licensed amateur radio operators may substitute five QSL cards as evidence of contacts with five amateur radio operators. (b) Option B, Radio Broadcasting. Do ALL of the following: (1) Discuss with your counselor FCC broadcast regulations. Include power levels, frequencies, and the regulations for low-power stations. (2) Prepare a program schedule for radio station "KBSA" of exactly one-half hour, including music, news, commercials, and proper station identification. Record your program on audiotape or in a digital audio format, using proper techniques. (3) Listen to and properly log 15 broadcast stations. Determine the program format and target audience for five of these stations. (4) Explain to your counselor at least eight terms used in commercial broadcasting, such as segue, cut, fade, continuity, remote, Emergency Alert System, network, cue, dead air, PSA, and playlist. (5) Discuss with your counselor alternative radio platforms such as internet streaming, satellite radio, and podcasts. (c) Option C, Shortwave and Medium-Wave Listening. Do ALL of the following: (1) Listen across several shortwave bands for four one-hour periods-at least one period during daylight hours and at least one period at night. Log the stations properly and locate them geographically on a map, globe, or web-based mapping service. (2) Listen to several medium-wave stations for two one-hour periods, one period during daylight hours and one period at night. Log the stations properly and locate them on a map, globe, or web-based mapping service. (3) Compare your daytime and nighttime logs; note the frequencies on which your selected stations were loudest during each session. Explain differences in the signal strength from one period to the next. (4) Compare your medium-wave broadcast station logs and explain why some distant stations are heard at your location only during the night. (5) Demonstrate listening to a radio broadcast using a smartphone/cell phone. Include international broadcasts in your demonstration. (d) Option D, Amateur Radio Direction Finding. Do ALL of the following: (1) Describe amateur radio direction finding and explain why direction finding is important as both an activity and in competition. (2) Describe what frequencies and equipment are used for ARDF or fox hunting. (3) Build a simple directional antenna for either of the two frequencies used in ARDF. (4) Participate in a simple fox hunt using your antenna along with a provided receiver. (5) Show, on a map, how you located the "fox" using your receiver. (e) Option E, Family Radio Service (FRS) and General Mobile Radio Service (GMRS) Walkie Talkies. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain what the Family Radio Service (FRS) and General Mobile Radio Service (GMRS) are and how they are different from each other, from other commercial two-way radios, and from Citizens Band (CB) and amateur radio (ham). (2) Explain each of the following for using a FRS radio or GMRS walkie talkie: (a) Is any type of license needed to use these radios? If so: what kind? (b) What radio frequencies are used and how is information encoded? (c) How much power can be used when transmitting? (d) What type of antenna can be used? (e) What is the effective range and what limits it? (f) What are common everyday uses for these radios? (g) How can these radios be useful in an emergency? (3) Use the FRS radios or GMRS walkie talkies with family, friends, or Scouts on a hike, at an event, or in a team game. Discuss what you learned with your counselor.

requirements.req_text: Careers. Do ONE of the following: (a) Explore careers related to radio. Research one career to learn about the training and education needed, costs, job prospects, salary, job duties, and advancement. With permission of your parent or guardian, your research methods may include an internet or library search, an interview with a professional in the field, or a visit to a location where people in this career work or train. Discuss your findings and career interest with your counselor. (b) Explore how you could use radio knowledge and skills to develop a hobby or to serve as a volunteer. If possible, with permission of your parent or guardian, interview a radio hobbyist or volunteer. Research training and licensing needed, expenses, and organizations that promote or support your objectives. Discuss with your counselor what short-term and long-term goals you might have if you pursue this.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What is the single most critical safety rule when choosing a location to erect an outdoor amateur radio mast or wire antenna?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What is the single most critical safety rule when choosing a location to erect an outdoor amateur radio mast or wire antenna?
options: A. Mount the antenna directly onto an electric utility pole so the coax shield shares the power company ground wire.
B. String dipole wires directly underneath high-voltage overhead distribution lines to shield the receiver from lightning.
C. Erect the mast only during rainstorms so moist soil improves radio-frequency grounding.
D. Locate the antenna and mast far enough from all overhead power lines that even if the mast or wire falls in any direction, it cannot come within 10 feet of a power line.
choices: A. Mount the antenna directly onto an electric utility pole so the coax shield shares the power company ground wire.
B. String dipole wires directly underneath high-voltage overhead distribution lines to shield the receiver from lightning.
C. Erect the mast only during rainstorms so moist soil improves radio-frequency grounding.
D. Locate the antenna and mast far enough from all overhead power lines that even if the mast or wire falls in any direction, it cannot come within 10 feet of a power line.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Locate the antenna and mast far enough from all overhead power lines that even if the mast or wire falls in any direction, it cannot come within 10 feet of a power line.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Contact between an antenna or mast and overhead electrical power lines is a leading cause of fatal electrocution in radio operations; antennas must never be placed where they could fall onto or near power lines.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why are local police and public safety radio systems typically assigned frequencies in the VHF and UHF portions of the spectrum?
options: A. VHF and UHF signals bounce off the ionosphere to reach other continents easily
B. VHF and UHF transmitters do not require antennas to send voice messages
C. VHF and UHF bands provide reliable short-range coverage suited for local jurisdictions
D. VHF and UHF frequencies can only carry Morse code instead of voice audio
choices: A. VHF and UHF signals bounce off the ionosphere to reach other continents easily
B. VHF and UHF transmitters do not require antennas to send voice messages
C. VHF and UHF bands provide reliable short-range coverage suited for local jurisdictions
D. VHF and UHF frequencies can only carry Morse code instead of voice audio
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. VHF and UHF bands provide reliable short-range coverage suited for local jurisdictions
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Radio services are matched to frequencies whose physical behavior fits their mission, and VHF and UHF bands are ideal for reliable short-range local police communications (p. 20).

choices: A. Enough specific logged details about the broadcast program, date, and time to prove reception

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How does a continuous wave (CW) transmitter encode Morse code messages onto a radio signal?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How does a continuous wave (CW) transmitter encode Morse code messages onto a radio signal?
options: A. By rapidly hopping between fifty different UHF channels every second
B. By keeping the carrier amplitude constant while stereo music plays in the background
C. By transmitting light pulses through an underground glass fiber cable
D. By switching the radio carrier wave on and off to create dits and dahs
choices: A. By rapidly hopping between fifty different UHF channels every second
B. By keeping the carrier amplitude constant while stereo music plays in the background
C. By transmitting light pulses through an underground glass fiber cable
D. By switching the radio carrier wave on and off to create dits and dahs
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. By switching the radio carrier wave on and off to create dits and dahs
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Continuous wave (CW) is a simple encoding system where the transmitter keys the carrier wave on and off to represent Morse code dits and dahs (p. 29).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: In a radio station block diagram, what is the role of the coaxial feed line?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: In a radio station block diagram, what is the role of the coaxial feed line?
options: A. It converts human speech into electrical audio signals before the microphone
B. It connects the transceiver or amplifier to the antenna to carry radio signals between them
C. It replaces the schematic diagram by listing every resistor value inside the power supply
D. It broadcasts NOAA weather warning tones directly to the operator's speaker without a receiver
choices: A. It converts human speech into electrical audio signals before the microphone
B. It connects the transceiver or amplifier to the antenna to carry radio signals between them
C. It replaces the schematic diagram by listing every resistor value inside the power supply
D. It broadcasts NOAA weather warning tones directly to the operator's speaker without a receiver
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. It connects the transceiver or amplifier to the antenna to carry radio signals between them
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): In a radio station, the feed line is the transmission cable that connects the transceiver and amplifier to the antenna so signals can travel to and from the radiating element (p. 27).

options: A. It changes from an amateur call sign to a commercial broadcast call sign at sunset
B. It increases transmitter power when sent in lowercase letters
C. It means a question when followed by a question mark and a statement without one
D. It encrypts the transmission so only FCC inspectors can decode the text
choices: A. It changes from an amateur call sign to a commercial broadcast call sign at sunset
B. It increases transmitter power when sent in lowercase letters
C. It means a question when followed by a question mark and a statement without one
D. It encrypts the transmission so only FCC inspectors can decode the text
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. It means a question when followed by a question mark and a statement without one
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Each three-letter Q-signal carries two meanings: sending it with a question mark asks a standard question, and sending it alone makes the corresponding statement (p. 10).
